title: Native API
summary: Native API execution means malware drives the operating system through its own programming interfaces instead of running a separate attacker supplied binary. Applications call documented entry points such as process creation and memory allocation routines, which in turn reach kernel services; the same end result can also be requested by invoking system calls directly from assembly, skipping the user mode libraries that many security products hook. Code can be injected into an already running process, so the new behaviour appears under a process the user and the monitoring stack already trust, and no obviously malicious executable needs to sit on disk. Detection therefore rests on context instead of signature: Windows Security 4688 and Sysmon process creation events expose odd parent child relationships, image load records show unusual libraries inside ordinary processes, and memory scans surface executable regions that no file on disk explains. The calls themselves are entirely legitimate, which is exactly why they blend in.

beginner.definition: The native API is the set of built in functions that programs use. They ask the operating system to do things, such as start a process or set aside memory. This technique means an attacker uses those functions directly to run their own actions. The operating system does the work, so no separate attack tool needs to run.
beginner.whyItMatters: The calls are normal and the operating system must allow them. So you cannot easily block the technique itself. Malicious behaviour can appear inside a process you already trust, such as a document reader or a chat program. Some attackers also bypass the library hooks that security tools use to watch these calls. That makes protection depend on context, not on a list of bad names.
howItWorks: A program calls a low level function, for example one that starts a new process.
The request passes kernel services that manage memory, devices and running programs.
Attackers inject code into an already trusted process so the work hides there.
Skilled attackers write their own assembly to call the kernel directly, avoiding monitored libraries.
The result is a real action, such as running a command, with no attacker file on disk.
Defenders see ordinary functions used in unusual places, by processes that should not use them.
beginner.example: A hotel has a front desk for guests and a hidden service corridor for staff. Guests never see the corridor, yet staff move luggage and prepare rooms through it all day. A dishonest staff member uses the same corridor. The lobby camera records nothing unusual, because nobody needed to walk through the lobby at all.
takeaways: Native API execution does not require a new file; it reuses the operating system itself.
The calls are legitimate, so detection is about context, not about a suspicious function name.
Process creation, image load and memory records are where this behaviour becomes visible.

objectives: Describe what the native API is and why applications rely on it for low level operations.
Explain how attackers use API calls, syscalls and code injection to execute behaviour.
Identify the Windows and Linux telemetry sources that record process creation and loaded modules.
Explain why user mode API hooks can be bypassed and what that means for detection coverage.
Judge suspicious API use by process context rather than by function names alone.
